1.title: Analyze Data
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Analyze Data. This module covers the task statement: analyze data by using a w s services. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Visualize data with Amazon QuickSight (Amazon Quick), DataBrew and other tools. Verify and clean data with Lambda, Athena, QuickSight, Jupyter notebooks and SageMaker Data Wrangler. Use S Q L in Amazon Redshift and Athena to query data and create views. Explore data with Athena notebooks that use Apache Spark. Describe the trade-offs between provisioned and serverless services. Define aggregation, rolling average, grouping and pivoting.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Builds Dashboards
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Builds Dashboards. Operations wants a live on-time-delivery dashboard. Finance wants monthly cost by route, refreshed each morning. Engineers want pipeline health on a time-series chart. Your job: pick the visualization tool and the data path for each.

1.title: Visualizing Data
1.text: Visualizing Data. Amazon QuickSight (now part of Amazon Quick). Best for: Business intelligence dashboards, ad hoc analysis, embedded analytics, M L (machine learning) insights. Remember: Serverless; Spice (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) for fast imported data or direct query; sources Athena (S three), Redshift, R D S (Relational Database Service), Aurora, OpenSearch and many more; row-level security; pay per user or session. A W S Glue DataBrew. Best for: Visual profiling of a dataset (distributions, missing values, correlations). Remember: For preparation, not dashboards. Amazon Managed Grafana. Best for: Operational and time-series dashboards. Remember: Managed Grafana for CloudWatch, Prometheus, OpenSearch, Timestream and more. OpenSearch Dashboards. Best for: Log and event exploration. Remember: Included with Amazon OpenSearch Service.

1.title: Visualizing Data, continued
1.text: Visualizing Data, continued. Jupyter notebooks (SageMaker, E M R (Elastic MapReduce) Studio, Athena). Best for: Exploratory analysis in code. Remember: Python, S Q L, charts. QuickSight data path: datasets (from a source or S Q L query) to Spice import (fast, scheduled refresh, up to the capacity) or direct query (always current, slower, loads the source) to analyses to dashboards shared with readers. Athena as a source lets QuickSight chart S three data lakes through the Glue Data Catalog. Exam tip: "Interactive dashboards on S three data, no servers" to QuickSight with Athena. "Time-series operational metrics" to Managed Grafana.

1.title: Verifying and Cleaning Data
1.text: Verifying and Cleaning Data. The figure shows this: Ways to verify and clean data: Lambda for small event-driven checks, Athena S Q L for set-based checks, DataBrew or Data Wrangler for visual steps, notebooks for code, and QuickSight charts to spot outliers.

1.title: Verifying and Cleaning Data, continued
1.text: Verifying and Cleaning Data, continued. A W S Lambda. Small, event-driven checks on arriving files or records (schema, ranges, formats); reject or fix. Amazon Athena. S Q L checks over S three data: counts, nulls, duplicates, outliers, referential checks; C T A S (create table as select) to write a clean copy. Amazon QuickSight. Charts and filters reveal gaps, spikes and odd categories. Jupyter notebooks. Python (pandas, PySpark) for exploratory cleaning. Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler. Visual data preparation for M L and analytics inside SageMaker (profiles, hundreds of built-in transforms, quality insights). A W S Glue DataBrew. Profile and clean visually (Module ten).

1.title: Verifying and Cleaning Data, continued
1.text: Verifying and Cleaning Data, continued. Common cleaning tasks: remove duplicates, handle nulls (drop, fill, flag), fix types and formats, standardize units, case and time zones, trim and parse text, validate against rules, detect and treat outliers. Verify with row counts before and after, checksums, sample comparisons and data quality rules (Module thirteen).

1.title: SQL in Amazon Redshift and Athena
1.text: S Q L in Amazon Redshift and Athena. Both use A N S I (American National Standards Institute)-style S Q L: select, J O I N, group by, having, order by, subqueries and C T E s (common table expression) (W I T H), window functions, set operations. Views: a view saves a query. Athena views are logical (stored in the Glue Data Catalog, run each time). Redshift views are logical, with late-binding views that do not depend on the underlying objects at creation (needed for Spectrum external tables); materialized views store results (Module six). Athena S Q L runs on S three data (Trino and Presto based); Redshift S Q L runs on warehouse tables and Spectrum external tables (PostgreSQL based).

1.title: SQL in Amazon Redshift and Athena, continued
1.text: S Q L in Amazon Redshift and Athena, continued. Use views for: reusable logic, hiding columns or rows, stable names over changing tables, simplifying joins for analysts. Performance habits: select only needed columns, filter on partition and sort keys, join on distribution keys, avoid select on wide columnar data.

1.title: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting
1.text: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting. Aggregation: combine many rows into one value: count, sum, avg, min, max. Grouping: group by makes one result row per group (per route, per month); having filters groups after aggregation, where filters rows before. Window function: calculates across related rows without collapsing them: over (partition by... order by...). Rolling (moving) average: an average over a sliding window, such as the last seven days, to smooth noise and show trends.

1.title: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting, continued
1.text: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting, continued
1.text: Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting, continued. Pivoting: turn row values into columns (months across the top) for reports; in Redshift use pivot, in Athena use conditional aggregation (sum(case when month equals 'Jan' then cost end)); unpivot does the reverse. Related ideas: running total (sum(...) over (order by...)), rank (rank, row number), percentiles, cube and rollup subtotals. Exam tip: "Smooth daily values with the average of the last seven days" to a window function with a rolling frame. "Show months as columns" to pivot.

2.title: Athena Notebooks with Apache Spark
2.text: Athena Notebooks with Apache Spark. Amazon Athena for Apache Spark runs interactive Spark without clusters: you work in notebooks (in the Athena console or SageMaker Unified Studio) with sessions that start in seconds. Write PySpark or Spark S Q L to explore, join, reshape and chart data in S three, using the Glue Data Catalog; no infrastructure to manage, pay for compute while the session runs. Use it when: S Q L alone is not enough (custom Python, machine-learning-style prep, complex reshaping) but you do not want an E M R cluster. Compare: Athena S Q L equals simple, per-data-scanned; Athena Spark equals code and exploration, serverless; E M R or Glue equals production pipelines at scale. Exam tip: "Explore S three data with PySpark in a notebook and no cluster to manage" to Athena notebooks with Apache Spark.

2.title: Provisioned versus Serverless
2.text: Provisioned versus Serverless. The figure shows this: Provisioned versus serverless: provisioned for steady, predictable workloads with full control; serverless for spiky, unpredictable or occasional workloads with no capacity planning.

2.title: Provisioned versus Serverless, continued
2.text: Provisioned versus Serverless, continued. Capacity. Provisioned: You choose size and count. Serverless: Automatic scaling. Cost shape. Provisioned: Pay while it exists (reserved or committed discounts possible). Serverless: Pay for use; nothing when idle. Best for. Provisioned: Steady, predictable, heavy workloads. Serverless: Spiky, unpredictable, occasional or new workloads. Control. Provisioned: Tuning, versions, instance types. Serverless: Less control. Drawbacks. Provisioned: Over- or under-provisioning, operations. Serverless: Startup or cold-start time, limits and quotas, can cost more at constant high use.

2.title: Provisioned versus Serverless, continued
2.text: Provisioned versus Serverless, continued. Data warehouse. Provisioned option: Redshift provisioned (R A three). Serverless option: Redshift Serverless. Big data processing. Provisioned option: E M R on E C two (Elastic Compute Cloud). Serverless option: E M R Serverless, A W S Glue. S Q L on S three. Provisioned option: Redshift Spectrum on a cluster. Serverless option: Athena. Streaming. Provisioned option: Kinesis provisioned shards, M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) Provisioned. Serverless option: Kinesis on-demand, M S K Serverless. Relational. Provisioned option: R D S, Aurora provisioned. Serverless option: Aurora Serverless version two. Key-value. Provisioned option: DynamoDB provisioned. Serverless option: DynamoDB on-demand. Search. Provisioned option: OpenSearch Service domains. Serverless option: OpenSearch Serverless. Exam tip: "Unpredictable or spiky analytics, pay only when queries run" to Redshift Serverless or Athena. "Constant heavy workload with predictable cost" to provisioned with reserved capacity.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Visualization: QuickSight (Amazon Quick): serverless B I (business intelligence), Spice or direct query, Athena or Redshift sources, R L S (row-level security). Cleaning: Lambda (small, event), Athena S Q L (set-based checks, C T A S), DataBrew or Data Wrangler (visual), notebooks (code), QuickSight (spot outliers). S Q L: Views (logical; Redshift late-binding for Spectrum), materialized views store results; select columns, filter keys. Aggregation: group by (rows to groups), having (filter groups), windows (over), rolling average (rows between n preceding and current row), pivot (Redshift pivot; Athena case). Athena Spark: Serverless notebooks, PySpark or Spark S Q L, no cluster, pay while the session runs. Provisioned versus serverless: Provisioned: steady, control, idle cost. Serverless: spiky, no planning, pay for use, startup and limits.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Operations at Kestrel Freight want interactive dashboards on data in an S three data lake, shared with many readers, with no servers to manage. Which combination fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. QuickSight is a serverless B I service, and Athena exposes S three data through the Glue Data Catalog.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. An analyst needs the average delivery delay for the last seven days, calculated for each day, to smooth daily noise. Which S Q L approach is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A window function with a rolling frame computes a moving average without collapsing rows.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A report must show months as columns with total cost per route in the rows, using Athena. Which technique should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Pivoting turns row values into columns; Athena does this with conditional aggregation.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A data scientist wants to explore data in S three with PySpark in a notebook without managing a cluster. Which service feature fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Athena for Apache Spark provides serverless interactive Spark sessions in notebooks over data in S three.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Select two. A company has unpredictable, occasional heavy analytics and does not want to pay for idle capacity. Which two options match? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Both are serverless and charge for use, so there is no idle cost. The other options keep paying for capacity.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A team wants reusable query logic that hides columns from analysts and gives stable names over changing tables in Athena. What should they create? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A view stores a query as a reusable logical table, can expose only selected columns and gives a stable name.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: B. Question four: C. Question five: D and E. Question six: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
